reference.source: Standard breast surgery textbook and benign breast disease guidance
clinicalPearls: Duct ectasia is dilatation and shortening of the major subareolar ducts, most often seen in peri- and postmenopausal women
The typical presentation is nipple discharge, which is frequently thick, cheesy, and green, grey, or brown, and may involve multiple ducts and both breasts
Other features include a palpable subareolar thickening or lump, nipple tenderness, and slit-like nipple retraction as periductal fibrosis develops
Because nipple retraction and a subareolar mass can mimic malignancy, triple assessment is used to reach a confident benign diagnosis
It is distinguished from lactational conditions by its non-lactational context and from periductal mastitis, an associated inflammatory process more common in younger smokers
Bloodstained or single-duct discharge is not typical and should prompt exclusion of an intraductal papilloma or carcinoma
Most cases need only reassurance and symptomatic measures once malignancy is excluded, as the condition often settles
Surgery, such as excision of the affected ducts, is reserved for troublesome persistent discharge, recurrent infection, or diagnostic uncertainty
reference.pathophysiology: Duct ectasia involves progressive dilatation of the large ducts beneath the nipple, with accumulation of inspissated secretions and periductal inflammation. The stagnant luminal contents and leakage of material into surrounding tissue provoke a chronic inflammatory and fibrotic response, which over time shortens and scars the ducts. This fibrosis can tether and retract the nipple and produce a firm subareolar mass, features that clinically overlap with carcinoma. The condition is degenerative and age-related and is closely related to periductal mastitis, in which the inflammatory component predominates and is strongly linked to smoking.
additionalDifferentials: Breast carcinoma, including ductal carcinoma in situ
Lactational or other physiological nipple discharge
Fibroadenoma or other benign subareolar mass
additionalInvestigations: Clinical examination of the nipple, discharge, and subareolar region as part of triple assessment
Mammography in women of appropriate age
Assessment of nipple discharge, with testing for blood where relevant
Ductography or ductoscopy in selected cases of troublesome single-duct discharge
Core biopsy of any discrete or suspicious mass
redFlags: Bloodstained or single-duct discharge suggesting papilloma or malignancy
A hard, irregular, or fixed mass or skin change
Nipple retraction with other features raising concern for carcinoma
reference.prognosis: Duct ectasia is a benign condition with a good prognosis; symptoms frequently settle with conservative management, and surgery is curative for persistent discharge, although periductal inflammation can recur, particularly in smokers.
pitfalls: Attributing nipple retraction or a subareolar mass to duct ectasia without excluding carcinoma
Overlooking bloodstained or single-duct discharge that requires further investigation
Failing to advise smoking cessation where periductal mastitis coexists
Rushing to surgery before completing triple assessment
Confusing physiological discharge with pathological discharge
references: Standard breast surgery reference text on benign breast disease
Guidance on nipple discharge and periductal disease
management: Reassure and manage conservatively once triple assessment has confirmed a benign diagnosis, as symptoms frequently settle without surgery
Advise warm compresses, good nipple hygiene and supportive measures for nipple discharge and subareolar tenderness
Strongly encourage smoking cessation, particularly where associated periductal mastitis is present
Reserve antibiotics with anaerobic cover, such as co-amoxiclav, for superimposed periductal infection or abscess
Offer total duct excision (Hadfield procedure) or microdochectomy for persistent, troublesome or recurrent nipple discharge
Investigate bloodstained or single-duct discharge and any discrete mass with imaging and core biopsy to exclude an intraductal papilloma or carcinoma
